opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the short answer is that individual neurons just aren't the right unit of analysis. The intuitive hope early on was that you'd open up a network, look at neuron 4,000-whatever, and find it's the "dog neuron" or the "Golden Gate Bridge neuron." Occasionally you do get lucky. But most of the time, when you look at what makes a neuron fire, it's this grab bag of unrelated things: academic citations, Korean text, HTTP requests, and pictures of cats, all lighting up the same unit. We call that polysemanticity.

The reason it happens, we think, is superposition. The model wants to represent far more concepts than it has neurons, so it crams them in. If you have a high-dimensional space, you can fit many more almost-orthogonal directions than you have dimensions, especially when the features are sparse, meaning any given concept is only active a tiny fraction of the time. The model can tolerate a little interference between features because they rarely co-occur. So concepts get smeared across many neurons, and each neuron participates in many concepts. Looking at one neuron is like looking at one pixel and trying to figure out what the image is.

That's why I frame it as reverse engineering. You have to recover the actual features the model is using, which are directions in activation space, not the basis the neurons happen to give you. Tools like sparse autoencoders, or dictionary learning, let you decompose those activations into a much larger set of features that are far more interpretable and monosemantic. Then, and this is the really exciting part, you can ask how those features connect to each other across layers. What reads from what, what writes to what. That's where you get circuits: an actual description of the algorithm the network is running.

It's a bit like the difference between staring at individual transistors in a CPU and decompiling the program it's executing. The transistors are real, but the meaning lives at a different level of abstraction. And if we ultimately care about questions like "is this model being deceptive?" or "why did it make that decision?", we need the program, not the voltages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short answer is that individual neurons just aren't the right unit of analysis. People assumed for a long time that if you looked at a single neuron, it would correspond to one clean concept. Like, this is the cat neuron, this is the Golden Gate Bridge neuron. And sometimes you get lucky and that's true. But the vast majority of the time, when you look at what actually makes a neuron fire, it's this grab bag. It fires on Shakespeare, and on Python code, and on some specific chemistry term, and there's no coherent story.

The reason for that is what we call superposition. The model has way more concepts it wants to represent than it has neurons. If you've got, say, a few thousand neurons in a layer, but the world has millions of distinct features in it, the model is forced to compress. So it ends up packing many features into the same neurons, spread out in different directions in activation space, and relying on the fact that most of them are sparse, that they don't co-occur very often, so the interference is tolerable.

Once you accept that, looking at a neuron in isolation is sort of like trying to understand a compressed file by reading individual bytes. The information is there, but it's been scrambled across units in a way that isn't legible if you only inspect one at a time.

So the move is to say, okay, what are the actual computational pieces? What are the directions, the features, that the model is really using? And then, more importantly, how do those features connect to each other? Because a single feature firing isn't that interesting on its own. What's interesting is: this feature detects the subject of the sentence, it passes that forward, this other feature combines it with the verb, and together they produce the prediction. That's a circuit. That's a little algorithm the model learned.

And the thing that's compelling to me is that this is the only level of description where you can actually make claims about behavior. If I tell you neuron 4,021 lights up on cats, you can't do much with that. But if I can show you the chain of computation that goes from input to output, then I can say things like, this is why the model gave this answer, or this is where the reasoning went wrong, or this is the piece that would fire if the model were trying to deceive you. That's what you need for safety. You need to be able to audit the computation, not just catalog the parts.

The analogy I like is that it's genuinely reverse engineering. Someone hands you a compiled binary, no source code, no comments, and you're trying to recover what program it's running. You wouldn't do that by staring at individual bits in memory. You'd try to find the functions, figure out what they take as input, what they return, how they call each other. Neural networks are the same, except the compiler was gradient descent and it had no interest whatsoever in making the result readable to humans.

r002.rationale: It describes more features than neurons, but does not state that capacity is insufficient for predicting the next token across internet text.

r003.rationale: It explains that the model has more concepts than neurons, so it compresses by packing many features into the same neurons.

r004.rationale: It describes neurons as firing for unrelated items and says inspecting a neuron in isolation yields no coherent story, making interpretation difficult.

astra-6.text:
Because a neuron’s behavior doesn’t tell you, by itself, what role it plays in producing an answer. You might find a neuron that activates on some concept, and that’s useful, but you still want to know: What caused it to activate? What does that activation affect downstream? How does the network use that information?

There’s also no guarantee that the units we want to understand line up with individual neurons. A concept might be represented across many neurons, and a single neuron might participate in representing multiple concepts. So looking at neurons one at a time can give you a misleading picture of how the model works.

What we’re ultimately after is a causal account of the computation: how information gets represented, how it gets transformed, and how those transformations produce the output. Ideally, that account lets you make predictions—if I change this internal representation, the model’s answer should change in this particular way—and then test them. Individual neurons are evidence toward that explanation, but labeling them isn’t the explanation itself.

r003.rationale: It says a neuron may represent multiple concepts, but does not explain that limited capacity pressures neurons to serve multiple functions.

r004.rationale: It explains that one neuron can participate in multiple concepts, so examining neurons individually can give a misleading picture of how the model works.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the thing we’re trying to explain is how the network produces its behavior. A neuron’s activation is one observation about that process. Even if you can say, “This neuron responds to dogs,” you haven’t explained how the network recognizes a dog, or what it does with that information afterward.

And there isn’t necessarily a clean correspondence between neurons and concepts. A concept can be represented across many neurons, and an individual neuron can participate in representing multiple concepts. So looking at neurons one at a time can give you a misleading picture of the underlying computation.

What you really want is to identify the features the network represents, understand how those features interact, and trace how they contribute to an output. Then you can intervene: if I remove this feature or change this intermediate result, does the output change in the way my explanation predicts? That’s how you move from an interesting correlation to a causal account of what the network is doing.
